title: Long‐Term Associations Between Early Spatial Cognition and Academic Achievement
abstract: Abstract Mounting evidence suggests a close link between spatial and mathematical thinking. Previous longitudinal research (Frick, 2019) demonstrated that spatial transformation skills assessed at kindergarten age predicted children's mathematics performance in second grade. The present study builds on this work by examining long‐term academic outcomes up to the end of primary school. Parents of 42 of the 119 children in the original cohort provided school reports for grades 3–6. Results showed that spatial abilities assessed at the end of kindergarten explained a stable but nonsignificant amount of variance in visual arts and design marks across primary school. In contrast, the predictive value of spatial abilities for mathematics marks increased significantly from middle to late primary school, from 1.5% explained variance in grades 3–4 to 17.6% in grades 5–6, and this association held when class membership was taken into account. The absence of comparable effects for German language marks underscores the specificity of these associations. The results of this follow‐up study indicate a long‐term relation between early spatial abilities and later success in school mathematics. In addition, they refine accounts of spatial–mathematical associations by suggesting an increased relevance of spatial cognition from middle to late primary school.
